# Nutrient Dosing Cycles

Nutrient dosing cycles refer to the scheduled intervals when precise nutrient mixtures are supplied to crops within closed-loop vertical farming systems. These cycles ensure plants consistently receive essential elements like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, tailored to their growth stage.

Typically, dosing occurs every 4 to 6 hours, controlled by automated pumps linked to sensors measuring solution pH, electrical conductivity, and plant uptake rates. This regular delivery maintains optimal nutrient concentration and prevents accumulation or depletion.

Tradeoffs include balancing nutrient stability against system complexity and energy use. Frequent dosing improves accuracy but increases operational costs and pump wear.

For example, a grow tower with 500 plants doses 1.2 liters of a solution containing 150 ppm nitrogen every 5 hours, totaling 5.76 liters daily. Consistency avoids nutrient stress, boosting yield projections by 8%.

Common failures involve pump clogging, sensor drift causing overdosing, and timing errors leading to nutrient imbalances.
